f6.original_source_line: To obtain a Dirichlet twist one may use the inherited Washington Theorem14.1; its final page was not reacquired here. The following replacement uses the final published Milne ADT already inspected: I.1.3 and1.6(c), pp.18–19, give global reciprocity for the idele class group, compatible with the local maps. Composing the finite character delta with reciprocity gives a finite continuous idele-class character. The connected positive real component acts trivially. Every rational idele class has a representative whose finite components lie in product Z_p*, unique after choosing positive real component; this follows by multiplying by the rational product of its finite uniformizer powers. A finite continuous character of that compact product factors through (Z/rZ)* for some r. Write lambda for this idele-class character. In the decomposition C_Q=R_>0 times product Z_p*, the idele which is a uniformizer q at q and1 elsewhere is represented, after multiplication by q^-1, by positive real component1/q and finite units q^-1 at every p!=q and1 at q. Therefore, with arithmetic reciprocity, define eta on (Z/rZ)* to be the inverse of lambda restricted to the finite units; then eta(q)=delta(Frob_q) for q prime to r. If the published reciprocity convention is inverse arithmetic, invert that reciprocity map first. This retains the necessary inverse on the finite-unit character rather than silently reversing the twist. This derivation uses neither Washington's unreacquired page nor an unpublished theorem.

Every rational idele class has a representative whose finite components lie in `product Z_p^{*}`, unique after choosing positive real component; this follows by multiplying by the rational product of its finite uniformizer powers. A finite continuous character of that compact product factors through `(Z/rZ)^{*}` for some r. This retains the necessary inverse on the finite-unit character rather than silently reversing the twist. This derivation uses neither Washington's unreacquired page nor an unpublished theorem.

additional_source_lines.original_source_line: For an explicit check of the archimedean determinant scalar, choose symplectic integral cycles and normalized holomorphic forms `ω1,…,ωg`; write their period matrix `(1,τ)`. Riemann's bilinear identity gives their Gram matrix `Im τ`. The analytic Jacobian is `C^g/(Z^g+τZ^g)` and Abel–Jacobi pulls `dz_i` to `ω_i`. The positive volume of its fundamental parallelepiped is `det Im τ`, so the squared norm of `dz1∧…∧dzg` in the positive top-form convention is exactly `det Im τ`, also the squared determinant norm of the `ω_i`. The top-form integral uses the usual positive ordering of real pairs; changing between block and interleaved complex wedges accounts for the orientation sign, not a positive metric scalar. No `g!`, `π^g`, polarization degree, or isogeny degree occurs. A Kähler form raised to its gth power would require a factorial, but that is not this norm.

additional_source_lines.original_source_line: Here is the complete local/global obstruction check. Use the constant-module squaring sequence 1 -> {±1} -> mu_infinity -> mu_infinity -> 1. By local reciprocity, a finite character of G_Qp has a character square root exactly when its character on Qp* does. The torsion factor of Qp* is cyclic of even order; its only obstruction is the value at -1. The valuation Z factor admits a finite-order square root. For odd p, squaring on the pro-p principal units is an automorphism; for p=2 the torsion-free factor 1+4Z_2 is procyclic and its generator's image may be given a square root of twice the order. Thus the criterion holds also at 2, with no omitted principal-unit obstruction. Local H²(G_Qp,{±1}) has two elements, by Kummer and the local Brauer invariant. The boundary of chi equals the sign class at every finite prime. The latter is zero outside T because its class inflates from the unramified local quotient, which has cohomological dimension one. The global Brauer injection and invariant-sum exact sequence determine the real invariant as well. See the final Milne ADT second edition, I.1.3/I.1.6(b,c), and the proof of II.2.1, printed 164, for the reciprocity and Brauer statements.
